short: A tax charged on making or selling particular goods, such as fuel, tobacco or alcohol, usually a fixed amount per unit.
kid: When a shop sells some special things, like fuel for cars, it has to give a little extra money to the people who run the country. That extra gets added to what you pay.
detail: Excise duty is a tax on the production or sale of specific goods, often set as a fixed amount per unit (rupees per litre) rather than a percentage of the price. In India, GST replaced most central excise in July 2017, but petrol, diesel, aviation turbine fuel, crude oil and natural gas stay outside GST, so the Centre still levies excise on them while states add VAT on top; states also levy excise on liquor. Fuel excise is a major revenue lever: governments tend to raise it when crude is cheap and cut it to cool pump prices, which moves the fiscal deficit, inflation and the earnings of oil marketing companies. Rates change often, so check the latest notification rather than any fixed figure. Common confusion: excise is charged on goods made or sold at home, while customs duty is charged on imports.
example: Say the central excise on a litre of diesel is ₹15 and the country sells 9,000 crore litres in a year. The Centre collects ₹15 × 9,000 crore = ₹1,35,000 crore, or ₹1.35 lakh crore. A ₹2 cut per litre would cost it ₹18,000 crore a year.
formula: Excise collected = Duty per unit × Units sold (for a per-unit duty)

short: The tax a company pays on its profits, worked out on taxable profit after allowed expenses, not on its sales.
kid: A lemonade stand counts what is left after buying lemons and sugar. The people who run the town ask for a small part of those leftovers to pay for roads and parks.
detail: Corporate tax, or corporation tax, is a direct tax on a company's taxable profit, which is profit computed under tax law rather than the accounting profit in the annual report. In India, a 2019 reform let domestic companies pay a base rate of 22% (about 25.17% after surcharge and cess) if they give up most exemptions, while companies staying in the older regime pay higher base rates; the US federal rate has been 21% since 2018. These are rules as of 2025 and can change with any budget. Corporate tax drives net profit, cash flow and valuation, and rate cuts often lift stock markets because more profit reaches shareholders. Investors watch the effective tax rate, tax charged divided by profit before tax, which can differ sharply from the headline rate because of deductions, carried-forward losses and deferred tax. Common confusion: the tax is on profit, not on revenue.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns taxable profit of ₹100 crore and pays the 22% base rate plus a 10% surcharge and 4% cess. Its rate is 22% × 1.10 × 1.04 = 25.168%, so tax is about ₹25.17 crore and profit after tax about ₹74.83 crore.
formula: Corporate tax = Taxable profit × Tax rate (including any surcharge and cess)

short: A floor tax on a company's reported profit, so firms that shrink taxable income with big deductions still pay some tax.
kid: Some children find clever reasons to skip helping with chores. A house rule says everyone must still help at least a little bit.
detail: Minimum alternate tax (MAT), under Section 115JB of India's Income-tax Act, 1961, makes a company pay the higher of its normal tax and a percentage of its book profit, the profit shown in its audited accounts after specified adjustments. It targeted 'zero-tax companies' that reported healthy profits to shareholders while using exemptions and accelerated depreciation to show little taxable income. Under the rules as of 2025, the MAT rate is 15% plus surcharge and cess, and companies that opt for the 22% concessional regime are outside MAT. Tax paid under MAT above normal tax becomes MAT credit, usable within a time limit in later years when normal tax exceeds MAT. Analysts track unused MAT credit because it can keep a company in the old regime. The US has a similar 15% minimum tax on the book income of very large companies. The Income-tax Act, 2025 renumbers the section.
example: Say XYZ Ltd reports book profit of ₹200 crore but, after deductions, taxable income of only ₹40 crore. Normal tax at 30% would be ₹12 crore, while MAT at 15% of book profit is ₹30 crore, so it pays ₹30 crore (before surcharge and cess) and carries forward ₹18 crore of MAT credit.
formula: Tax payable = Higher of (Normal tax on taxable income, MAT rate × Book profit)

short: A one-off or temporary extra tax on companies that earn unusually large profits from events they did not cause, such as a price spike.
kid: If a big wind blows lots of apples into one child's garden, the grown-ups might ask that child to share some apples with everyone, because it was luck, not hard work.
detail: A windfall tax targets profits that jump because of outside events, such as a war-driven surge in oil or gas prices, rather than better management. Governments use it to fund relief for consumers or to keep scarce supplies at home. After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the UK introduced an Energy Profits Levy and the EU a 'solidarity contribution' on energy firms. India imposed a special additional excise duty (SAED) from July 2022 on domestically produced crude oil and on exports of petrol, diesel and jet fuel, revising it every fortnight in line with global prices, and scrapped it in December 2024. For investors, windfall taxes cap the upside in commodity stocks and raise policy risk, which can weigh on valuations even after the tax ends. Common confusion: it taxes extra profit, not all profit, though deciding what counts as 'extra' is a political choice.
example: Say the government sets a levy of ₹2,000 per tonne on domestic crude while oil prices are high, and a producer, say ABC Oil Ltd, pumps 10 lakh tonnes in a quarter. It pays 10,00,000 × ₹2,000 = ₹200 crore for that quarter.

short: A tax law that applies to deals or income from the past, changing the tax owed on events already completed under older rules.
kid: Imagine you finished a game and won. Then someone changes the rules afterwards and says you owe a sweet for that old game. That feels unfair.
detail: Retrospective taxation means a law changed today that applies to earlier years, so a transaction done legally under old rules can suddenly carry tax, interest and penalties. India's best-known case followed Vodafone's 2007 purchase of Hutchison's Indian mobile business through an offshore company. The Supreme Court ruled in 2012 that the deal was not taxable in India, but the Finance Act 2012 changed the law retrospectively to tax such indirect transfers of Indian assets. Vodafone and Cairn Energy then won international arbitration awards against India in 2020. In 2021 Parliament withdrew demands based on that amendment for transfers before 28 May 2012 and refunded tax collected, without interest. The episode is still cited as a blow to policy certainty and foreign investment. Common confusion: clarifying an unclear law is different from creating a new tax for the past, though governments often describe the second as the first.
example: Say in 2026 a hypothetical company, XYZ Holdings, is told that a 2018 sale which produced a ₹500 crore gain, untaxed under the law at the time, is now taxable at 20%. It faces a ₹100 crore demand for an eight-year-old deal, before any interest.

short: Legally reducing your tax by using deductions, exemptions or gaps the law allows; it turns aggressive when deals exist only to save tax.
kid: The house rules say you can skip one chore if you tidy your toys first, so you tidy your toys. That is allowed, because you followed the rules.
detail: Tax avoidance is lowering tax within the letter of the law: investing in tax-saving schemes, timing the sale of assets, or choosing where to locate a business. Ordinary tax planning is accepted, but aggressive avoidance uses artificial steps, such as shell companies or round-trip deals, that have little purpose beyond the tax saving. Many countries counter this with general anti-avoidance rules. India's GAAR, in force since April 2017, lets tax authorities ignore an 'impermissible avoidance arrangement' whose main purpose is a tax benefit and that lacks commercial substance; under the rules as of 2025 it applies only when the benefit in a year exceeds ₹3 crore. For investors, a company's heavy reliance on aggressive structures is a risk, because a successful challenge brings back-tax and penalties. Common confusion: avoidance is legal, if sometimes challenged, while tax evasion, hiding income or faking records, is a crime.
example: Under India's old regime for FY 2025-26, say Rohan invests ₹1,50,000 in an ELSS fund, a deduction allowed under Section 80C. In the 30% slab this cuts his tax by ₹45,000 before cess: legal avoidance. Hiding ₹1,50,000 of rent income instead would be evasion.

short: Illegally paying less tax than owed, by hiding income, inflating expenses or faking records; a crime that brings penalties and prosecution.
kid: If you hide some of your sweets behind your back so you do not have to share them as you promised, that is cheating, and you get into trouble.
detail: Tax evasion is deliberately breaking the law to cut tax: not reporting income, keeping cash sales off the books, claiming fake expenses, issuing bogus invoices to claim input tax credit, or keeping money abroad undeclared. Unaccounted income of this kind is what Indian news calls 'black money'. Penalties are steep. Under India's rules as of 2025, under-reported income attracts a penalty of 50% of the tax evaded and misreported income 200%, on top of the tax and interest, and prosecution is possible; the Black Money Act, 2015 separately targets undisclosed foreign income and assets. The Annual Information Statement, GST e-invoicing and automatic exchange of bank data between countries have made evasion easier to detect. For the economy, widespread evasion shrinks the tax base and pushes the burden onto honest taxpayers. Common confusion: tax avoidance uses the law, while evasion breaks it.
example: Say a shop owner hides ₹10 lakh of sales and, at a 30% rate, skips ₹3 lakh of tax. If caught and the income is treated as misreported, he owes the ₹3 lakh plus a 200% penalty of ₹6 lakh, so ₹9 lakh before interest.

short: A country or territory with very low or no taxes and often secrecy, used to park profits or wealth away from higher-tax countries.
kid: Imagine a toy box in a friend's house where nobody asks you to share. Some people put their toys there so they do not have to share at home.
detail: A tax haven, or offshore financial centre, offers very low or zero tax, light reporting rules and, historically, strong secrecy, which attracts holding companies, funds and wealthy individuals. Well-known examples include the Cayman Islands, Bermuda and the British Virgin Islands. Multinationals can shift profit there by placing intellectual property or financing arms in the haven and charging high fees to group companies elsewhere. Leaks such as the Panama Papers (2016) and Pandora Papers (2021), automatic exchange of bank information and the 15% global minimum tax have reduced both the secrecy and the benefit. In India, much foreign investment came through Mauritius and Singapore because their tax treaties exempted capital gains, until both treaties were amended in 2016. Common confusion: using a low-tax centre is not automatically illegal; it becomes evasion when income or assets are hidden from the authorities.
example: Say Globex Inc, a hypothetical group, books $100 million of profit in a zero-tax territory instead of a country taxing it at 25%. It saves $25 million. Under a 15% global minimum tax, a $15 million top-up could be collected, cutting the saving to $10 million.

short: The prices that companies in the same group charge each other for goods, services or loans, which tax authorities require to match market prices.
kid: Two brothers swap toys. If one pretends a tiny car is worth a giant castle, it is not a fair swap, so a grown-up checks that swaps are fair.
detail: Transfer pricing covers deals between related entities, such as an Indian subsidiary paying its foreign parent for royalties, software, management services or interest. Because the group controls both sides, it could shift profit to the lower-tax country by setting the price too high or too low. Tax laws therefore require an arm's length price (ALP), the price unrelated parties would agree in similar conditions, found using methods such as comparable uncontrolled price, cost plus or the transactional net margin method. In India the rules sit in Sections 92 to 92F of the 1961 Act, a Transfer Pricing Officer can adjust income, and companies can seek an Advance Pricing Agreement for certainty. Transfer pricing disputes are among the largest tax cases for multinationals and IT services firms. Common confusion: the term is about pricing between group entities for tax, not about what a company charges its customers.
example: Say ABC India Ltd pays its Singapore parent a royalty of ₹1,200 per unit when an arm's length royalty is ₹1,000, on 5 lakh units. The excess is ₹200 × 5,00,000 = ₹10 crore, which the tax officer adds back to Indian income; at a 25% tax rate that is ₹2.5 crore of extra tax.
formula: Adjustment to income = (Price paid to related party - Arm's length price) × Units

short: A treaty between two countries that stops the same income being taxed fully in both, by deciding which country taxes it or giving credit.
kid: If two friends both ask you for a piece of the same cookie, they agree a rule first, so you never have to give away the same piece twice.
detail: A Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA), or tax treaty, decides which of two countries may tax cross-border income such as dividends, interest, royalties, capital gains and business profits, and caps the tax the source country can withhold. Where both may tax, the country of residence gives relief by exempting the income or crediting the foreign tax paid. India has comprehensive treaties with more than 80 countries; to claim treaty rates, a non-resident usually needs a Tax Residency Certificate from its home country. Treaties shaped India's capital flows: Mauritius and Singapore became top routes for foreign investment because they exempted capital gains, until 2016 protocols let India tax gains on shares bought after April 2017. Anti-abuse tests, such as the principal purpose test, now deny benefits to shell entities. Common confusion: a treaty can only reduce tax; it cannot create a tax that domestic law does not impose.
example: Say domestic law would withhold 20% on interest paid to a foreign lender, but the treaty caps it at 10%. On ₹10 lakh of interest, tax in India falls from ₹2 lakh to ₹1 lakh, and the lender's home country gives credit for the ₹1 lakh already paid.

short: Tax that the payer deducts from a payment, such as salary, interest or dividends, and sends to the government before paying the rest.
kid: When grandpa gives you pocket money, he first keeps a coin aside for the family jar and gives you the rest.
detail: Withholding tax is collected at the source: the person or company making a payment holds back part of it and deposits it with the government in the recipient's name. It is used worldwide for wages, interest, dividends, royalties and payments to foreigners, because collecting from one payer is easier than chasing many recipients. India's version is TDS (tax deducted at source); payments to non-residents fall under Section 195 of the 1961 Act, and a tax treaty may lower the rate. The recipient can usually claim the withheld amount as a credit against final tax, so it often works as an advance payment rather than an extra tax. For investors, withholding on cross-border dividends and bond coupons reduces the net yield, which is why foreign investors watch treaty rates closely. Common confusion: withholding is a way of collecting tax, not a separate type of tax.
example: Say an Indian company pays ₹10 lakh of interest to a foreign lender and the applicable withholding rate is 20%. It deposits ₹2 lakh with the government and pays the lender ₹8 lakh, and the lender can usually claim the ₹2 lakh as a credit at home.
formula: Tax withheld = Gross payment × Withholding rate; Net paid = Gross payment - Tax withheld

short: An international agreement that large multinational groups should pay at least 15% tax on profits in every country where they operate.
kid: Friends agree that everyone must put at least one sweet in the shared jar. Nobody can hide their sweets in another room to skip it.
detail: The global minimum tax is Pillar Two of the OECD/G20 project on base erosion and profit shifting (BEPS), agreed in 2021 by more than 130 countries. It applies to multinational groups with annual revenue of at least €750 million. If a group's effective tax rate in any country falls below 15%, a top-up tax is charged, first by that country through a domestic top-up tax if it has one, otherwise by the parent's country or others under backstop rules. The EU, UK, Japan, South Korea and many others began applying it from 2024. In 2025 the G7 backed a 'side-by-side' approach that largely spares US-headquartered groups, so the system is still evolving. It reduces the gain from tax havens and generous tax incentives. Common confusion: Pillar One, a separate proposal, reallocates taxing rights to the countries where customers are, and is not the 15% minimum.
example: Say a hypothetical group, Globex, books $200 million of profit in a country where it pays $10 million of tax, an effective rate of 5%. Ignoring carve-outs, top-up tax = (15% - 5%) × $200 million = $20 million.
formula: Top-up tax = (15% - Effective tax rate in the country) × Excess profit, where Excess profit = Profit - Substance-based carve-out

short: A former Indian tax on payments to foreign digital companies, such as for online ads, aimed at tech giants with no local office.
kid: A big toy shop far away sells lots of toys to children in your town but never helps your town. So your town asked for a little share each time someone bought from it.
detail: India's equalisation levy, nicknamed the Google tax, was introduced in 2016 at 6% on payments by Indian businesses to non-resident firms for online advertising, deducted by the payer. In 2020 a 2% levy was added on the revenue of foreign e-commerce operators selling to Indian users. The idea was to tax digital firms that earn large sums in India without a permanent establishment, which treaties normally require before business profits can be taxed. Both were wound down as global tax talks progressed and US trade pressure grew: the 2% levy was abolished from August 2024 and the 6% levy from April 2025. Similar digital services taxes exist in France, the UK and other countries. Common confusion: the levy sat outside the Income-tax Act, so foreign firms could not always claim credit for it at home, unlike regular income tax.
example: Under the old 6% levy, say an Indian retailer paid ₹50 lakh to a foreign platform for online ads. It deducted ₹50,00,000 × 6% = ₹3 lakh, deposited that with the government, and paid the platform ₹47 lakh.
formula: Levy = Payment for the specified digital service × Levy rate

short: A former Indian tax on startups that raised money at a share price above the shares' official fair value, treating the excess as income.
kid: If a friend gives you ten sweets for a toy that is only worth five, a grown-up once said the five extra sweets were a present you had to share.
detail: Angel tax was the popular name for Section 56(2)(viib) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. When a closely held company issued shares at a price above their fair market value, the excess was taxed as the company's 'income from other sources'. The aim was to stop money laundering through inflated share issues, but it hit genuine startups, whose valuations rest on future growth that formula-based fair value methods ignore. Recognised startups won exemptions from 2019, while the Finance Act 2023 extended the rule to money raised from foreign investors, prompting protests from founders and venture capital funds. The Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 abolished it for all investors from financial year 2024-25. Startup investors still cite it as an example of policy risk. Common confusion: the tax fell on the startup that raised the money, not on the angel investor.
example: Say a hypothetical startup, Byteloop, issued 1 lakh shares at ₹100 each while their fair value was worked out at ₹60. The excess of ₹40 × 1,00,000 = ₹40 lakh would have been taxed as the startup's income under the old rule.
formula: Taxable excess = (Issue price - Fair market value) × Shares issued

short: A tax on the property and money a person leaves behind when they die, paid from the estate before heirs receive it.
kid: When someone grows very old and dies, their things are passed on to their family. In some countries, a small part goes to everyone's shared pot first.
detail: An estate tax is charged on the total value of a dead person's estate, above an exempt amount, before it passes to heirs; an inheritance tax is similar but is charged on what each heir receives, sometimes at rates that depend on the relationship. Both are often called death duties. The US has a federal estate tax with a top rate of 40% and a very high exemption, and the UK charges inheritance tax at 40% above a threshold, under rules as of 2025. India had an estate duty from 1953 but abolished it in 1985 because it raised little and was costly to collect. Today heirs in India pay no tax on receiving an inheritance, though they pay capital gains tax when they later sell inherited assets, using the original owner's cost. Common confusion: gift tax covers transfers made while alive, while estate tax covers transfers at death.
example: Say a country exempts the first $15 million of an estate and taxes the rest at 40%. An estate worth $20 million pays 40% × $5 million = $2 million, so the heirs share $18 million.
formula: Estate tax = (Value of estate - Exemption) × Tax rate

short: Simplifying the Goods and Services Tax rate structure by merging rate slabs and moving items to lower or higher rates.
kid: Imagine a sweet shop with lots of different kinds of price tags. The owner decides to use just a few kinds, so everyone can understand them easily.
detail: GST rate rationalisation means reshaping India's GST rate structure so that fewer, simpler rates apply and oddities such as inverted duty structures disappear. The biggest round, often called GST 2.0, was approved by the GST Council in September 2025 and took effect on 22 September 2025: the main slabs of 5%, 12%, 18% and 28% gave way to two main rates of 5% and 18%, plus a 40% rate for a short list of luxury and 'sin' goods, and compensation cess was removed from most goods. Many daily-use items, small cars and appliances became cheaper, which economists expected to lift consumption and ease inflation, at some cost to tax revenue. Consumer, auto and FMCG stocks reacted strongly to the announcement. Rates can change again at later council meetings. Common confusion: rationalisation can raise rates on some items even while it cuts most.
example: Say a product costs ₹1,000 before tax. At 12% GST the buyer pays ₹1,120; if the product moves to the 5% slab, the buyer pays ₹1,050, a saving of ₹70, or 6.25% of the old price.
formula: Price paid = Pre-tax price × (1 + GST rate)

short: The three parts of India's GST: central and state GST shared equally on sales within a state, and integrated GST on sales between states.
kid: When you buy a toy in your own town, the helper money is split between your town and the whole country. When the toy comes from another town, the country collects it first and later passes your town its part.
detail: India's GST is a dual tax, levied by both the Centre and the states on the same transaction. On a sale within a state, the rate is split equally into Central GST (CGST), kept by the Centre, and State GST (SGST), kept by that state; in union territories without a legislature, UTGST replaces SGST. On a sale from one state to another, and on imports, Integrated GST (IGST) is charged at the full rate and collected by the Centre, which then settles the state's share with the state where the goods or services are consumed, because GST is a destination-based tax. Input tax credit follows set rules: IGST credit can be used against any of the three, but CGST credit cannot pay SGST, or the other way round. Common confusion: the split does not change the total rate the buyer pays.
example: On a ₹10,000 sale taxed at 18% inside Maharashtra, the seller charges CGST of 9% (₹900) and SGST of 9% (₹900). If the same item is sold to a buyer in Karnataka, the seller charges IGST of 18%, or ₹1,800, so the buyer pays the same total either way.
formula: Within a state: CGST = SGST = (GST rate / 2) × Taxable value; Between states: IGST = GST rate × Taxable value

short: An extra GST-linked charge on luxury and harmful goods such as tobacco, created to make up states' revenue losses after GST began.
kid: When friends agreed to share one big piggy bank, some worried they would get less. So a little extra was collected on fancy treats to make sure nobody lost out.
detail: When GST began in July 2017, states gave up many of their own taxes, so the GST (Compensation to States) Act promised that for five years their protected revenue would grow 14% a year from a 2015-16 base, with any shortfall paid from a cess on goods such as tobacco, pan masala, aerated drinks, coal and cars. The promise ended in June 2022, but COVID-19 left a large gap, so the Centre borrowed about ₹2.69 lakh crore on behalf of states in 2020-21 and 2021-22 and extended the cess to March 2026 to repay those loans. With GST 2.0 in September 2025, the cess was removed from most goods and kept on tobacco products only until the loans are cleared. Common confusion: cess money is not shared through the Finance Commission formula; it was ring-fenced for compensating states.
example: Say a state collected ₹10,000 crore in 2015-16 from taxes later merged into GST. Its protected revenue for 2018-19, three years on, was ₹10,000 crore × 1.14 × 1.14 × 1.14 = ₹14,815.44 crore; if it actually collected ₹14,000 crore, it was owed ₹815.44 crore of compensation.
formula: Compensation = Protected revenue - Actual revenue, where Protected revenue = 2015-16 base revenue × 1.14^(years since 2015-16)

short: A situation where the tax or duty on a product's inputs is higher than the tax on the finished product, trapping cash for makers.
kid: Imagine you hand over lots of stickers to get beads, but when you trade your bead necklace you only collect a few stickers back. You are left waiting for the rest.
detail: An inverted duty structure arises when inputs are taxed at a higher rate than the output made from them. Under GST, a manufacturer pays tax on purchases and claims it as input tax credit against the tax due on sales; if the output rate is lower, credit piles up unused, tying up working capital. GST law allows a refund of such accumulated credit on inputs, though the Supreme Court in 2021 upheld the rule that leaves credit on input services out of the refund. In customs, inversion occurs when raw materials or components face a higher import duty than the finished product, which makes domestic manufacturing less competitive. Textiles, fertilisers and footwear were long-running examples, and rate rationalisation, including GST 2.0 in 2025, aimed to remove many of them. Common confusion: the problem is not a high tax rate as such but the mismatch between input and output rates.
example: Say a fabric maker buys ₹80 lakh of inputs taxed at 18%, paying ₹14.4 lakh of GST, and sells fabric worth ₹100 lakh taxed at 5%, owing ₹5 lakh. After using credit to pay the ₹5 lakh, ₹9.4 lakh of credit is stuck until a refund comes through.
formula: Accumulated credit = GST paid on inputs - GST payable on output (when positive)

short: The part of your income on which tax is actually charged, after subtracting the exemptions and deductions the law allows.
kid: You get ten sweets, but two are for your lunchbox and do not count. Only the other eight are the ones you have to share from.
detail: Taxable income is the figure your tax rates are applied to. In India, income is first sorted into five heads: salaries, income from house property, profits and gains of business or profession, capital gains, and income from other sources such as interest. Each head is computed under its own rules, losses are set off where allowed, and the sum is gross total income. Deductions such as Section 80C or 80D, mostly available under the old regime, are then subtracted to reach total income, the taxable amount, rounded to the nearest ₹10. Some income, such as agricultural income, is exempt from tax. For companies, taxable profit is accounting profit adjusted for items that tax law treats differently, which is why reported tax expense and cash tax can diverge. Common confusion: your salary or a company's revenue is not its taxable income; exemptions, deductions and expenses come off first.
example: Under the old regime for FY 2025-26, say Priya earns a salary of ₹15,00,000, takes the ₹50,000 standard deduction and earns ₹50,000 of bank interest, giving gross total income of ₹15,00,000. After a ₹1,50,000 Section 80C deduction, her taxable income is ₹13,50,000.
formula: Total income = Gross total income (sum of the five heads after set-offs) - Deductions under Chapter VI-A

short: The tax rate charged on your next rupee of income, which is usually higher than your average tax rate across all income.
kid: Your first few sweets are all yours to keep. But once you have lots, you share one out of every few new sweets you get.
detail: Under a progressive system, income is taxed in slabs, and each slab has its own rate. The marginal rate is the rate on the slab where your last rupee falls, while the average rate is total tax divided by total income, which is lower when the lower slabs are taxed less. The marginal rate is what matters for decisions: how much of a bonus, a pay rise or extra interest you keep, and how much a deduction saves you. India also uses marginal relief, which caps the extra tax when income crosses a threshold that triggers a surcharge or ends the Section 87A rebate, so earning slightly more never leaves you worse off. Slab rates change with budgets, so use the latest ones. Common confusion: moving into a higher slab does not raise the tax on all your income, only on the part above where that slab starts.
example: Under India's new regime slabs for FY 2025-26, tax on ₹20 lakh is ₹2,00,000 before cess, an average rate of 10%. Earning ₹1 lakh more adds ₹25,000 of tax because the next slab is taxed at 25%: that is the marginal rate.
formula: Marginal tax rate = Change in tax / Change in taxable income; Average tax rate = Total tax / Total taxable income

short: An Indian deduction for your own National Pension System contributions, currently up to ₹50,000 a year, on top of the Section 80C limit.
kid: If you put some coins in a special jar saved for when you are very old, your family lets you keep a few more of your coins today.
detail: Section 80CCD(1B), added in 2015, gives an extra deduction for an individual's own contributions to a National Pension System (NPS) Tier I account, up to ₹50,000 a year under the rules as of 2025. It sits outside the ₹1.5 lakh combined cap on Sections 80C, 80CCC and 80CCD(1), so a taxpayer can deduct up to ₹2 lakh in all, but only under the old regime. Separately, Section 80CCD(2) allows a deduction for the employer's NPS contribution, up to 14% of basic salary plus dearness allowance under the new regime, and 10% for most private-sector employees under the old one. NPS money is largely locked in until retirement, so the tax saving must be weighed against limited access to the money. The Income-tax Act, 2025 renumbers these sections. Common confusion: 80CCD(1B) is for your own contribution, while 80CCD(2) is for your employer's.
example: Say Arjun, in the 30% slab under the old regime, puts ₹50,000 into NPS Tier I. The deduction saves ₹50,000 × 30% = ₹15,000 of tax, or ₹15,600 including the 4% cess.
formula: Tax saved = Deduction claimed (up to the limit) × Marginal tax rate × (1 + Cess rate)

short: An Indian income tax deduction for interest paid on a loan taken to buy, build, repair or renovate a house.
kid: When a family borrows to buy a home, they pay back a little extra each year as a thank-you. The country lets them keep some of their own money to help with that.
detail: Section 24(b) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 lets you deduct interest on a loan taken to buy, build, repair or rebuild a house, under the head 'income from house property'. For a home you live in, the deduction is capped at ₹2 lakh a year under the old regime, or ₹30,000 in some cases, such as repair loans or construction not completed within five years. For a rented-out property, interest is deductible in full against rent, but the resulting loss that can be set off against other income is capped at ₹2 lakh a year, with the rest carried forward for eight years. The new regime gives no deduction for a home you live in, though interest on a rented property still reduces rental income. Limits are as of 2025. Common confusion: principal repayment is a separate deduction under Section 80C.
example: Say Meera pays ₹2,60,000 of home loan interest in a year on the flat she lives in. Under the old regime she can deduct only ₹2,00,000; in the 30% slab that saves ₹60,000 before cess.
formula: Deduction for a self-occupied home = Lower of (Interest paid, ₹2 lakh cap under the old regime)

short: Money the tax department returns when tax already paid during the year, such as tax cut from salary, exceeds what you actually owed.
kid: You gave your teacher five coins for a school trip, but it only cost four. So the teacher gives you one coin back.
detail: A tax refund arises when prepaid taxes, such as tax deducted at source (TDS) by an employer or bank, tax collected at source, advance tax and self-assessment tax, add up to more than the final liability worked out in your return. Common reasons include TDS on interest when total income is below the taxable limit, or deductions claimed only at filing. In India a refund is issued only after the return is filed and processed, and it is credited to a pre-validated bank account linked to your PAN; delayed refunds usually earn simple interest, 0.5% a month under the rules as of 2025. At the national level, direct tax data are reported gross and net of refunds, and a surge in refunds can make net collections look weak. Common confusion: a refund is your own overpaid money coming back, not new income, though any interest on it is taxable.
example: Say ₹1,20,000 of TDS was deducted from Kavya's salary, but after her deductions her final tax works out to ₹95,000. She files her return and gets a refund of ₹1,20,000 - ₹95,000 = ₹25,000, plus any interest due.
formula: Refund = Taxes already paid (TDS + TCS + advance tax + self-assessment tax) - Final tax liability

short: A yearly summary on India's income tax portal of your financial transactions reported by banks, employers and others, used to check your return.
kid: Your teacher keeps a notebook of every star sticker you earned this year. At the end, you can check it to make sure nothing is missing or wrong.
detail: The Annual Information Statement (AIS), launched on the income tax e-filing portal in November 2021, gathers what third parties report about you for a financial year: salary and TDS, savings and deposit interest, dividends, share and mutual fund trades, property purchases, large cash deposits, foreign remittances and more. The Taxpayer Information Summary (TIS) condenses it into totals by category, and the department uses those values to prefill returns. Form 26AS still shows tax credits such as TDS and advance tax. Taxpayers can give feedback when an entry is wrong or duplicated. Because the department matches returns against AIS data automatically, income missing from a return can trigger a notice, a mismatch email or a delayed refund. Common confusion: AIS shows what others reported about you and can contain errors, so your return should show your correct income rather than blindly copying AIS.
example: Say Rahul's AIS shows ₹42,000 of savings and deposit interest from two banks, but his draft return shows ₹30,000 because he forgot one account. He should report the full ₹42,000, or he risks a notice on the ₹12,000 gap.

short: An Indian tax return (ITR-U) that lets you report income you missed in earlier years, by paying the tax due plus an extra charge.
kid: If you forgot to share some sweets last week, you can still bring them now, plus one extra sweet for being late, and everything is fine again.
detail: An updated return, filed in form ITR-U under Section 139(8A) of the 1961 Act, was introduced in 2022 so taxpayers could report income left out of earlier returns without penalty proceedings. Under the rules as of 2025, it can be filed up to 48 months from the end of the relevant assessment year, with additional tax of 25%, 50%, 60% or 70% of the extra tax and interest, depending on whether it is filed in the first, second, third or fourth year. It cannot be filed after a search or survey has begun. It differs from a belated return, filed after the due date but before the year-end cut-off with a late fee, and a revised return, filed by that cut-off to fix mistakes in a return already filed. Common confusion: ITR-U can only add tax; it cannot lower tax or claim a refund.
example: Say Neha forgot ₹1,00,000 of interest income and is in the 30% slab. Filing ITR-U within 12 months, she pays the ₹30,000 tax plus 25% additional tax of ₹7,500, so ₹37,500, ignoring interest and cess.
formula: Amount payable = (Extra tax + Interest) × (1 + Additional tax rate of 25%, 50%, 60% or 70%)

short: The 12-month period whose income is taxed together; in India it runs April to March, and the term replaced 'previous year' from April 2026.
kid: Every year you count how many stars you earned from one birthday to the next. The tax year is the grown-ups' counting time for their earnings.
detail: A tax year is the period for which income is measured and taxed. The UK's runs from 6 April to 5 April, and the US uses the calendar year for most individuals. India's Income-tax Act, 1961 used two labels: income was earned in the 'previous year', the April-March financial year, and assessed in the following 'assessment year', which confused many taxpayers. The Income-tax Act, 2025, in force from 1 April 2026, replaces both with a single 'tax year', the financial year in which the income is earned. Returns, deadlines and rate tables for income earned from April 2026 refer to the tax year, while older years keep the old labels. When reading news, filings or past returns, check which label a year uses before comparing figures. Common confusion: under the old labels, assessment year 2026-27 meant income earned in 2025-26, one year earlier.
example: Under the 1961 Act, salary earned from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 belonged to previous year 2025-26 and was assessed in assessment year 2026-27. Under the 2025 Act, income earned from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027 is simply tax year 2026-27.

short: A rule that lets existing investments, contracts or people keep the old treatment when a new law or tax comes in.
kid: When the family makes a new bedtime rule, big brother who always stayed up later keeps his old bedtime. The new rule is only for the younger ones.
detail: Grandfathering protects positions taken before a rule changed, so the new law applies only going forward. It reduces the sense of unfairness and the risk of a market sell-off when taxes rise. India's best-known case is long-term capital gains on listed equity: when the 2018 Budget brought this tax back, gains made up to 31 January 2018 were grandfathered by treating the higher of the actual cost and the 31 January 2018 price, capped at the sale price, as the cost. Grandfathering also protected investments made through Mauritius and Singapore before April 2017 when those tax treaties changed, and debt fund units bought before 1 April 2023 kept long-term capital gains treatment when rules changed that year. Investors should check grandfathering dates before selling old holdings. Common confusion: grandfathering freezes the old treatment only for what existed before the cut-off; new purchases follow the new rule.
example: Say Anil bought shares at ₹100 in 2016; they were ₹150 on 31 January 2018, and he sold them at ₹200 in 2025. His cost is taken as ₹150, so his taxable gain is ₹50 per share rather than ₹100.
formula: Grandfathered cost (listed equity) = Higher of (Actual cost, Lower of (Price on 31 January 2018, Sale price))

short: Indian tax relief that exempts long-term capital gains if you reinvest them in a residential house or specified bonds within set time limits.
kid: If you swap your old toy house for coins and use those coins to get a new toy house, nobody asks you to share any of them.
detail: Sections 54, 54F and 54EC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 let individuals avoid long-term capital gains tax by reinvesting. Section 54 covers gains from selling a residential house: the gain is exempt to the extent it is invested in another house in India, bought within one year before or two years after the sale, or built within three years. Section 54F covers gains from other long-term assets, such as shares or land, but the whole net sale proceeds must go into a house for full exemption; otherwise relief is proportional. Section 54EC lets gains from land or buildings be put, within six months, into specified bonds of issuers such as NHAI or REC, up to ₹50 lakh a year, locked in for five years. Under the rules as of 2025, the house exemptions are capped at ₹10 crore. Common confusion: selling the new house within three years undoes the relief.
example: Say Vikram sells a flat with a long-term gain of ₹80 lakh and buys a new flat for ₹60 lakh within two years. Under Section 54, ₹60 lakh of the gain is exempt and the remaining ₹20 lakh is taxable, unless he puts ₹20 lakh into 54EC bonds within six months of the sale.
formula: Section 54 exemption = Lower of (Long-term capital gain, Cost of new house); Section 54F exemption = Gain × Amount invested / Net sale consideration

short: A Hindu joint family that Indian tax law treats as a separate taxpayer, with its own tax number, income and tax slabs.
kid: A whole family can share one big toy box that belongs to all of them together. The toy box has its own name tag, separate from each child's.
detail: A Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) consists of all people descended in a direct line from a common ancestor, along with their wives and unmarried daughters; Jain, Sikh and Buddhist families are covered too. The senior member, the karta, manages its affairs, and since a 2005 change in succession law daughters are coparceners with equal rights. An HUF can own property, run a business and invest, and the Income-tax Act taxes it as a separate 'person' with its own PAN, basic exemption limit and deductions. Families use it to spread income across one more taxpayer and lower the overall tax rate. However, clubbing rules can add income from members' gifts back to the giver, and dissolving an HUF through partition is legally complex. Common confusion: an HUF arises by birth and marriage, not by registration, though it needs a PAN and a bank account to operate for tax.
example: Say a family's investments, held through its HUF, earn ₹6 lakh of taxable income in FY 2025-26. Added to the karta's income in the 30% slab, it would cost ₹1,80,000 in tax; in the HUF's own hands under the new regime, it is ₹2 lakh × 5% = ₹10,000, before cess.

short: A simple Indian scheme where small businesses and professionals declare a fixed share of their sales or fees as profit, without detailed accounts.
kid: Instead of counting every coin your lemonade stand made, you agree that a small fixed part of what you sold counts as your earnings, and share from that.
detail: Presumptive taxation spares small taxpayers from keeping full books and getting audits. Under Section 44AD of the 1961 Act, resident individuals, HUFs and partnership firms (not LLPs) with business turnover up to ₹2 crore, or ₹3 crore if cash receipts are no more than 5%, can declare 8% of turnover as profit, or 6% of receipts that come through banks or digital modes. Section 44ADA lets specified professionals, such as doctors, lawyers, architects and consultants, with receipts up to ₹50 lakh (₹75 lakh with limited cash) declare 50% as income. Section 44AE covers small goods transport operators. These limits are as of 2025. A business that leaves 44AD and declares lower profit cannot return to it for five years. Common confusion: you may declare more than the presumed rate, but declaring less usually requires full books and an audit.
example: Say a shop with ₹1.5 crore of turnover, all received digitally, opts for Section 44AD. Its presumed profit is ₹1.5 crore × 6% = ₹9 lakh. A consultant with ₹40 lakh of fees under Section 44ADA declares 50%, or ₹20 lakh.
formula: Presumptive income = Turnover or gross receipts × Prescribed rate (8% or 6% under 44AD, 50% under 44ADA)

short: Your tax category in a country, resident or non-resident, based mainly on days spent there, which decides whether foreign income is taxed.
kid: If you sleep at your grandma's house most nights, you follow her house rules. If you only visit sometimes, only a few of her rules apply to you.
detail: Residential status decides which income a country can tax. In India, an individual is resident in a financial year if present for 182 days or more, or for 60 days or more in the year plus 365 days over the previous four years; for Indian citizens and people of Indian origin visiting from abroad, the 60-day test becomes 182 days, or 120 days if Indian income exceeds ₹15 lakh. A resident is either 'ordinarily resident' or 'not ordinarily resident' (RNOR), mostly depending on how many recent years were spent abroad. Ordinary residents are taxed on worldwide income; non-residents (NRIs) and RNORs mainly on income earned or received in India. A citizen with Indian income above ₹15 lakh who is not taxed anywhere else can be a deemed resident. Thresholds are as of 2025. Common confusion: tax residency is separate from citizenship and from residence under foreign exchange law.
example: Say Emma, a British citizen, spends 100 days in India in FY 2025-26 and 400 days over the previous four years. She misses the 182-day test but meets the 60-day plus 365-day test, so she is resident in India for that year.

short: A tax on spending collected in stages, where each business pays tax only on the value it adds, and the final buyer bears it.
kid: A farmer grows wheat, a miller makes flour, and a baker bakes bread. Each one hands over a tiny share for the part they added, and it all adds up in the bread.
detail: Value-added tax (VAT) is charged at every step of production and sale, but each business deducts the tax it paid on purchases (input credit) from the tax it charges on sales, so only the value added at that step is taxed and the full burden falls on the final consumer. The credit chain also makes evasion harder, because buyers need sellers' invoices to claim credit. More than 170 countries use VAT, including the EU members and the UK; the US relies instead on state sales taxes. Indian states moved from sales tax to VAT around 2005, and in 2017 GST, a dual VAT, replaced it, but states still levy VAT on petrol, diesel and alcohol for drinking, which is why fuel prices differ across states. Rates vary widely by country and change over time. Common confusion: a sales tax is charged once at the final sale, with no credit chain.
example: With a 10% VAT, a farmer sells wheat for ₹100 and pays ₹10; a miller sells flour for ₹150 and pays ₹5 on the ₹50 added; a baker sells bread for ₹200 and pays ₹5 on the ₹50 added. Total VAT is ₹20, exactly 10% of the final ₹200 price.
formula: VAT payable = VAT on sales (output tax) - VAT on purchases (input tax)

short: A tax on money or property given away while alive; in India, the person receiving certain gifts may owe income tax on them.
kid: If a neighbour gives you lots of sweets, you may need to share some. But sweets from your own family are yours to keep.
detail: A gift tax stops people dodging income or estate taxes by giving assets away. Countries design it differently: in the US the giver pays federal gift tax, but only after large annual and lifetime exemptions. India abolished its Gift Tax Act in 1998 and since 2004 has taxed gifts in the receiver's hands as 'income from other sources', now under Section 56(2)(x) of the 1961 Act. Under the rules as of 2025, if gifts of money or property from non-relatives total more than ₹50,000 in a year, the entire amount is taxed at the receiver's slab rate. Gifts from defined relatives, on one's marriage, or by will or inheritance are exempt. Buying property or shares well below fair value can also be taxed as a gift. Common confusion: the ₹50,000 limit is a threshold, not a deduction, so crossing it by one rupee taxes the whole amount.
example: Say in one year Tanvi receives ₹40,000 from a friend, ₹30,000 from a colleague and ₹5 lakh from her father. The ₹70,000 from non-relatives crosses ₹50,000, so all ₹70,000 is taxable, while the ₹5 lakh from her father is exempt.
